computational_details.boundary_and_initial_conditions: Volume fraction of all phases (0.0-1.0) versus temperature (600-1500 °C) for the nominal alloy, used to design ~14 vol.% TiB2 embedded in a δ-ferrite + austenite matrix
computational_details.simulation_method: Equilibrium phase diagram (CALPHAD) calculation of phase fractions versus temperature
computational_details.validation_against_experiment: Designed TiB2 fraction ~14 vol.% (12.5 % measured by XRD; ~13 % by EBSD); ferrite-austenite dual-phase confirmed experimentally

analytical_models.equation_role: σ = σ0 + σgb + σdis (lattice friction + grain-boundary + dislocation strengthening)

analytical_models.model_note: Valid for both ferrite and austenite given their micrometer-scale grain sizes

analytical_models.equation_role: dρ/dε = M(k1√ρ - k2 ρ) - dislocation density evolution
analytical_models.model_note: k1 = athermal storage factor; k2 = dynamic recovery factor (constant at room temperature/constant strain rate)

analytical_models.equation_role: fd* = f0(1 - exp^-k((σeq-σc)/σc)^n) + fd0 - current volume fraction of damaged particles
analytical_models.model_note: Micro-mechanical interfaces modelled with zero-thickness COH3D8 cohesive elements governed by a bilinear traction-separation law calibrated against μ-DIC results

parameters.name: f0 (total proportion of potentially damageable particles)

computational_details.boundary_and_initial_conditions: 2D plane-strain RVE (CPE4 elements) mapped from a 200 μm × 200 μm EBSD image; mesh size 0.4 μm corresponding to 500 × 500 elements; periodic boundary conditions on boundary nodes (edges a, b, c, d), reference point RP-2 fixed and RP-1 stretched along the x-axis; TiB2 treated as linearly elastic (Orowan bypass not applicable to micron-sized boundary-localized particles)
computational_details.potential_model_or_database: Constitutive: Von Mises yield criterion with flow-stress decomposition (lattice friction + Hall-Petch grain-boundary strengthening + Taylor dislocation strengthening); Kocks-Mecking dislocation density evolution; Weibull-type particle fracture criterion; cohesive zone (bilinear traction-separation) for interfaces via COH3D8 zero-thickness elements
computational_details.simulation_method: Finite element method (FEM) using a two-dimensional plane-strain representative volume element (RVE)
computational_details.validation_against_experiment: Simulated true stress-strain curves and dislocation density evolution closely match experimentally measured curves (Fig. 11); parameter calibration used EBSD grain sizes, s-XRD dislocation densities, tensile curves and μ-DIC debonding results

analytical_models.equation_role: ΔK = 0.9/L + (πA^2b^2/2)^1/2 ρ^1/2 (K C̄^1/2) + O(K^2C̄) - relates peak broadening to crystallite size and dislocation density
analytical_models.model_note: Dislocation contrast factor C̄ = C̄h00(1 - q(h²k²+k²l²+h²l²)/(h²+k²+l²))

computational_details.boundary_and_initial_conditions: Diffraction peaks fit with pseudo-Voigt function; nine peaks for austenite and six for ferrite; peak broadening correlated with average coherent domain size L and dislocation density ρ
computational_details.potential_model_or_database: MWH method; dislocation contrast factor model (Ungár et al.); elastic constants for ferrite (C11=273 GPa, C12=110 GPa, C44=82 GPa) and austenite (C11=169 GPa, C12=82 GPa, C44=96 GPa); A set to 1
computational_details.simulation_method: Modified Williamson-Hall (MWH) line-profile analysis of synchrotron XRD data to calculate dislocation density
computational_details.validation_against_experiment: MWH plots (Fig. 10(c,d)) show high-quality linear fits; results used as initial dislocation density input (ρ0) for FEM

defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: Dislocation tangles occur at all TiB2/matrix interfaces regardless of particle size, consistent with the exclusive grain-boundary distribution of TiB2 particles; weak-beam BFTEM reveals detailed dislocation tangles at the δ-ferrite/TiB2 interface; the δ-ferrite/TiB2 interface shows denser dislocations than the austenite/TiB2 interface.

interfaces.interface_notes: δ-ferrite, initially formed during solidification, persisted throughout hot rolling and air cooling; the δ-ferrite/TiB2 interface is coherent/semi-coherent whereas the austenite/TiB2 and δ-ferrite/large-TiB2 interfaces show no clear orientation relationship.
interfaces.phase_evolution: No phase transformation from austenite to martensite occurred during the entire deformation process (volume fractions of austenite and δ-ferrite remain nearly constant).

phase_interfaces.coherence: coherent or semi-coherent interface; crystallographic orientation relationship {110}_δ-ferrite || {1-101}_TiB2 and <111>_δ-ferrite || <11-20>_TiB2 (from SADP along <11-20> zone axis of smaller TiB particle)

no clear crystallographic orientation relationship reported; weak-beam bright-field images show substantially lower dislocation densities at austenite/TiB2 interfaces than at δ-ferrite/TiB2 interfaces
banded/layered phase boundaries; strain incompatibility between soft austenite and hard δ-ferrite promotes geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs)

interfaces.slip_behavior: Local strain partitions among austenite (soft), δ-ferrite (hard) and TiB2; strain localizations distribute in multiregional bands (~45° to loading axis) rather than a single concentration. High local strain (~10 %) at small TiB2/δ-ferrite interface, elevated strain (~16 %) at austenite/TiB2 phase boundaries, and strain concentrations (~20 %) near sharp TiB2/austenite and TiB2/ferrite boundaries. The softer austenite accumulates higher local strain than δ-ferrite, while hard δ-ferrite deforms less.

comparative_performance.comparison_metric: σy increase of 22 % (503 MPa vs 389 MPa) and σu increase of 30 % (672 MPa vs ~549 MPa); uniform elongation of 13 % is higher than 11 % of the existing Fe-TiB2 steel; E (225 GPa) is 18 %–40 % higher than typical E (160–190 GPa) of Fe-Mn-Al-C type low-density steels; specific modulus 32.7 GPa g^-1 cm^3
comparative_performance.improvement_percentage: σy: 22%; σu: 30%; E: 18%–40% higher than Fe-Mn-Al-C LDSs

processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: A 50 kg cast ingot with the nominal composition Fe-15.5Mn-3.95Al-5Ti-2.15B (wt.%) was prepared using vacuum induction melting; the composition was chosen to allow ~14 vol.% TiB2 embedded in a δ-ferrite + austenite matrix (phase diagram calculations).
Cast into a rectangular ingot (per the Fig. 1(b) process schematic: Induction melting → Casting → Forging and homogenization → Hot rolling).
Forging stage preceding homogenization, as indicated in the Fig. 1(b) process schematic ('Forging and homogenization').
The ingot was homogenized at 1373 K for two hours prior to hot rolling.
Hot rolled in the two-phase region in five rolling steps with a finishing temperature of 1173 K to produce a 3 mm thick sheet.
processing_steps.reduction_ratio: reduced to a 3 mm thick sheet (five rolling steps, in the two-phase region)

processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Followed by air cooling to room temperature, giving the as-hot-rolled heterogeneous δ-ferrite + austenite + TiB2 microstructure.

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Density measured by hydrostatic weighing (Archimedes' principle) using an electronic densimeter; Young's modulus measured by impulse excitation technique with a solid material dynamic performance analyzer (resonant frequency analysis)
measurement_conditions.specimen_geometry: dog-bone tensile specimens, gauge length 25 mm, gauge width 6 mm, cut by electrical discharge machining with tensile axes parallel to the rolling direction; Young's modulus specimen 100 mm × 25 mm × 4 mm

tensile_properties.stress_strain_curves: Engineering stress-strain curve (red 'Our LDS') shown in Fig. 3(a): rises steeply, peaks just below 700 MPa at ~13-15 % strain and ends abruptly; simulated true stress-strain curve ends near 750 MPa at ~0.12-0.13 true strain (Fig. 11(a))

structures.microstructure_counts: Austenite ~59 % (EBSD area fraction), δ-ferrite ~28 % (EBSD), TiB2 ~13 % (EBSD); XRD volume fractions 62 % austenite, 26 % ferrite, 12.5 % TiB2. TiB2 area fraction estimated 9.6 % from RD surface and 13.4 % from ND surface.

structures.overall_structure: Heterogeneous triplex (composite) microstructure: a fully equiaxed-austenitic matrix embedded with elongated δ-ferrite bands/lamellae and micron-sized TiB2 particles. The matrix exhibits a typical banded or layered microstructure consisting of alternating lamellae of δ-ferrite and austenite aligned along the rolling direction; TiB2 particles (dark contrast) are randomly distributed in the metallic matrix.

structures.microstructure_counts: Austenite and δ-ferrite volume fractions remain nearly constant with tensile deformation (no phase transformation)

defects.dislocation_density: δ-ferrite: (1.7 ± 0.7) × 10^15 m^-2; austenite: (2 ± 0.3) × 10^15 m^-2 (after straining to fracture)
defects.lattice_distortion: KAM shows defects accumulate in both δ-ferrite and austenite after deformation

grain_structure.texture: GNDs generated due to soft/hard phase contrast between δ-ferrite and austenite

phases_present.morphology: deformed grains; dense dislocation tangles after straining
progressively fractured particles and particle/matrix decohesion with increasing strain

precipitates.distribution: particle fracture (dominant, especially large/agglomerated particles) and particle/matrix decohesion during tensile straining

microstructure_list.region: uniformly strained gauge area after tensile fracture

structures.overall_structure: Post-tensile-deformation microstructure of the same as-hot-rolled steel: phase map comparison shows the volume fractions of austenite and δ-ferrite remain nearly constant during deformation (no strain-induced austenite-to-martensite transformation); defects now accumulate in both δ-ferrite and austenite, in contrast to the initial state where defects existed predominantly in δ-ferrite.

unmapped_findings: The present as-hot-rolled low-density steel has a specific yield strength (SYS) of 73.1 MPa g^-1 cm^3 and specific ultimate tensile strength (SUTS) of 97.7 MPa g^-1 cm^3, owing to its low density.
Specific modulus (E/ρ) of the present steel is calculated to be 32.7 GPa g^-1 cm^3, remarkably higher than the typical ~25 GPa g^-1 cm^3 for light metals such as aluminum, magnesium, and titanium.

The present steel achieves a strength-ductility balance (SYS × UE value around 9-10 MPa g^-1 cm^3) positioned among existing ceramic-reinforcement steels while maintaining a high specific modulus (~32.7 GPa g^-1 cm^3, highest among the compared steels).

δ-ferrite contributes ~170 MPa (over 30 % of the overall yield strength) as a stable strengthening baseline, nearly constant throughout deformation, while the strengthening contribution from austenite increases with strain (Fig. 12(c)); the phase stress of δ-ferrite surpasses that of austenite by nearly 50 % in the elastic stage.
FEM-simulated phase stresses at ~830 MPa global true stress: TiB2 reaches ~1180 MPa (highest), δ-ferrite ~710 MPa, austenite ~670 MPa (lowest, softest phase).

Onset of yielding of the present steel (global true stress ~490 MPa, close to the measured σy) is attributed to plastic flow of austenite (micro-yielding), not δ-ferrite; above ~600 MPa both matrix phases flow plastically and TiB2 continues to bear increasing load via strain hardening of the matrix.

Damage evolution: first defect-containing particle fracture occurred at true plastic strain εp = 0.0069 and applied true stress σa = 556 MPa (exceeding σ0.2 = 503 MPa); cracks oriented nearly perpendicular to the tensile axis. Statistical analysis of 336 TiB particles (189 predominantly austenite-contacting, 147 ferrite-contacting) showed austenite-surrounded particles exhibited significantly higher fracture frequencies; particle fracture accelerates final failure more than particle decohesion.
Large particles (>10 μm) constitute >80 % of the volume fraction of TiB2 and dictate bulk mechanical behavior; small particles (0.8-5.0 μm) account for only 1.01 % of the volume fraction.
Fracture surface shows a mixed fracture mode comprising ductile dimples, quasi-cleavage fracture of TiB2 particles, and particle/matrix decohesion.

Austenite grains with GOS < 2° (fully recrystallized) account for 90.8 % (area fraction) of the austenite phase, while recrystallized δ-ferrite accounts for only 52.2 % of the ferrite phase, showing sluggish δ-ferrite recrystallization during hot rolling.
Average thickness of ferrite bands is 4.3 μm, smaller than that of austenite layers (12.1 μm).
